summary: This LibreTexts page, "Vision and Light" from the Biological Chemistry supplemental modules, explains how light triggers molecular change in the eye. It covers the visible spectrum, the conversion of vitamin A (retinol) to retinal, and the isomerization of 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal that starts the visual signal. It then describes how the resulting signal travels as an electrical impulse via rods and cones to the brain, which forms the image.
one_line: Explains how light isomerizes retinal in rhodopsin and how rods and cones pass visual signals to the brain.
key_facts: The visible spectrum is 400 nm to 700 nm.
Vitamin A, also known as retinol, is critical for vision because it is needed by the retina of the eye.
Retinol can be converted to retinal, and retinal is a chemical necessary for rhodopsin.
As light enters the eye, 11-cis-retinal is isomerized to the all-trans form.
The new all-trans-retinal form does not fit as well into the protein, so a series of geometry changes in the protein begins, forming a complex referred to as bathrhodopsin.
A lysine side-chain from the opsin reacts with 11-cis-retinal to form a linkage called a Schiff base.
The retina contains 7 million cones, which provide color information and sharpness of images.
The retina contains 120 million rods, which are extremely sensitive detectors of white light and provide night vision.
The tops of rods and cones contain membrane-bound discs holding cis-retinal bound to the protein opsin.
The cis-retinal bound to opsin is called rhodopsin or "visual purple".
As the protein changes geometry, a cascade of biochemical reactions builds a large potential difference across the plasma membrane.
The potential difference is passed to an adjoining nerve cell as an electrical impulse, which the nerve carries to the brain.
The brain determines which nerve fibers carried the impulse from activated photoreceptors and creates an image.
Signal transduction pathway is a mechanism describing the ways cells react and respond to stimulation.
The page cites L. Stryer's Biochemistry (W.H. Freeman and Co, 1975) and Rodney Cotterill's The Cambridge Guide to the Material World (Cambridge University Press, 1985) as references.
